opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of people frame it the wrong way. They look at it as "what am I giving up?" and they tally up the salary, the equity, the title, the next promotion. And those are real. I'm not going to pretend they aren't. But the question I kept coming back to was a different one: what's the risk of *not* doing it?

When I was at DeepMind working on the data center cooling work, I had what was, by any reasonable measure, a fantastic job. Brilliant colleagues, incredible resources, really interesting problems. But I'd seen something that I couldn't unsee, which was that you could take these AI control systems and apply them to real industrial infrastructure and get meaningful, measurable improvements in energy efficiency. And I became convinced that this was going to happen in the world one way or another. The question was just whether I was going to be part of making it happen, or whether I was going to watch from the sidelines.

So when I did the math, the downside scenario was actually pretty bounded. If the company fails, what happens? I spend a few years working incredibly hard on a problem I care about, I learn an enormous amount, and then I go get another job. The skills don't disappear. The network doesn't disappear. If anything, you come out more valuable than you went in. People drastically overestimate how permanent the damage of a failed startup is.

Whereas the regret scenario, that felt unbounded. Being sixty and thinking, "I had a window, I had the right expertise at the right moment, and I didn't take it." That's the one I couldn't live with.

The other thing I'd say is that timing matters a lot, and it's not just market timing, it's personal timing. There are seasons in life where your obligations are lighter and you can absorb more risk. If you're in one of those seasons and you have conviction about a problem, that's worth paying attention to, because those windows don't stay open forever.

And I'll be honest, conviction is the key word. I don't think you should leave a great job just because you want to "be a founder." That's not a good enough reason, because the hard days will absolutely break you. You need to be obsessed with the problem itself. For me, it was this idea that so much of the world's critical infrastructure is still run on fairly static, rules-based control, and there's this massive opportunity to make it more efficient and more reliable. That's what gets you out of bed when things are going sideways, and in a startup, things go sideways a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says that after a failed company the founder can get another job, and that the skills gained mean they may come out more valuable than they went in.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that I had the risk calculation almost exactly backwards when I was sitting at DeepMind thinking about this. I was framing it as, "I have this great job, I have this trajectory, and if I leave and the company fails, I've lost all of that." And that's the natural way to frame it, but it's wrong, because it treats the job as the safe, static thing and the startup as the risky thing.

What I eventually realized is that the job isn't actually safe either. The opportunity I was looking at, taking the work we'd done on data center cooling at Google and bringing that kind of AI optimization to industrial facilities more broadly, that window wasn't going to stay open forever. Someone was going to go do it. And if I stayed, in five years I'd still have a good job, but I'd be watching someone else build the thing I knew how to build. So the real risk wasn't "what if I leave and fail." It was "what if I stay and the thing I actually care about happens without me."

The second piece is being honest about what the downside actually looks like. If you leave a place like Google or DeepMind and your company doesn't work out, you are extremely employable. You've learned a huge amount, you've got a network, you've got a story. The floor is high. People imagine the downside as some kind of catastrophe, and for most people in that position, it really isn't. It's a couple of years of lower pay and a lot of stress, and then you're fine. Once I wrote that down concretely rather than feeling it as this vague dread, it got a lot less scary.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is who you're doing it with. I didn't leave alone. Vedavyas and I had worked together for years, we'd been through hard technical problems together, we trusted each other. That cuts the risk enormously, because so much of what kills early companies isn't the market, it's the founders falling apart. So if someone asked me how to assess the risk, I'd honestly say: spend less time on the spreadsheet and more time asking whether the problem will still matter in ten years, whether your downside is really as bad as it feels, and whether you'd want to be in the trenches with these specific people when things go wrong. Because they will go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says that after a failed company, the founder is still highly employable because they have learned a great deal, built a network, and gained a story to tell employers.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to get concrete about what you’re actually risking. A well-paid job and a promising career are valuable, so the opportunity cost is real. But leaving that job doesn’t necessarily mean giving up that career forever. If the company fails, can you get another job? What will you have learned? How much financial runway do you need, and who else depends on you?

I’d separate the risk of the company failing from the risk of the decision being a mistake. You can start a company that doesn’t work out and still come away with skills, relationships, and a much better understanding of what you want to do.

Then there’s the other side: what’s the cost of staying? If there’s a problem you really want to solve, and you have a credible reason to believe you can solve it, passing up that opportunity has a cost too. For me, the question would be whether the downside is manageable and whether the opportunity is compelling enough to justify taking it.

r001.rationale: The response says a failed venture can still provide skills and asks whether the founder could get another job, but it does not state that those skills increase the founder’s value to employers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to ask, what are you actually risking? A well-paid job is something tangible, so leaving it feels like a big loss. But staying has a cost too: you’re spending time you could have spent building something you really care about.

For me, it helps to make the downside concrete. If the company doesn’t work, can I recover financially? Can I find another job? What will I have learned along the way? That doesn’t make the risk disappear, but it makes it easier to reason about.

Then there’s a separate question: do I care enough about this problem to keep working on it when things get hard? A promising career is a good reason to stay. But if you have room to take the risk, and there’s a problem you feel compelled to solve, leaving can be a very reasonable decision.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether the founder could find another job and what they would learn, but does not state that skills gained from starting a company would increase their value to employers if it failed.
